prompt.brief: Design a batch and streaming data platform that ingests events from many sources, transforms them reliably, and serves fresh analytical results without losing data during backpressure or worker failure.
successSignals: Separate immutable raw data, replayable events, stateful stream processing, and query-optimized analytical tables.
Explain event-time windows, late data, watermarks, deduplication, schema evolution, and exactly-once effects.
Use one ingestion contract for streaming and batch backfills while isolating noisy tenants and hot keys.
Define data-quality gates, privacy controls, replay, dead-letter handling, and operational freshness metrics.

functional: Ingest events from APIs, message brokers, databases, and object-storage batch drops.
Validate schemas, normalize records, enrich them, and run windowed streaming and historical batch transformations.
Write raw immutable data and curated analytical tables for dashboards, ad-hoc queries, and exports.
Expose pipeline configuration, run status, freshness, quality failures, replay, backfill, and cancellation.
nonFunctional: Acknowledge accepted events after durable ingestion, not after every downstream table is updated.
Target p95 streaming freshness below 10 seconds for healthy partitions and make lag visible.
Preserve ordering where required by a business key while scaling independent partitions in parallel.
Make retries, late events, duplicate delivery, schema changes, partial sink failure, and regional recovery safe.
scaleAssumptions: Ingest 2 million events per second at peak, with records averaging 2 KB and 10x bursts.
Retain raw data for 90 days in object storage and curated data for years in a columnar warehouse.
Largest tenants can dominate a partition, so partition keys may require salting and tenant quotas.
A streaming job has hundreds of partitions and a batch backfill may run thousands of tasks.

dataFlow.title: Register sources and contracts
dataFlow.description: Connectors authenticate each source, validate schema compatibility and partition ownership, and persist a source manifest before ingestion.

dataFlow.title: Ingest with backpressure
dataFlow.description: Events enter partitioned durable buffers; producers receive bounded backpressure while failed records go to a replayable dead-letter path.

dataFlow.title: Process event time
dataFlow.description: Stream operators use checkpoints, watermarks, deduplication, and explicit late-data policy to produce windowed patterns and aggregates.

dataFlow.title: Publish analytical outputs
dataFlow.description: Batch and streaming sinks write versioned results and action intents only after the corresponding checkpoint and quality gates succeed.

dataFlow.title: Recover and reconcile
dataFlow.description: A failed worker resumes from a checkpoint, replays affected partitions, and compares sink counts and watermarks before declaring recovery.

architecture.title: Batch and streaming data platform reference architecture
architecture.summary: Durable ingestion feeds replayable raw storage and partitioned processing; quality-gated manifests publish curated data to analytical stores.

deepDives.title: Exactly-once effects and checkpoints
points: For the batch and streaming analytics platform, accepted offsets, checkpoint state, and sink writes must advance together.
Design for the failure case where a slow partition or failed worker must not silently advance a window or lose an event; keep retries, versions, and repair state explicit.
Expose freshness, version, lineage, or audit metadata so operators and clients can distinguish current, pending, and degraded state.

deepDives.title: Watermarks, late data, and backpressure
points: For the batch and streaming analytics platform, accepted offsets, checkpoint state, and sink writes must advance together.
Keep this concern off unrelated request paths and partition it by the batch and streaming analytics platform access key.
Expose freshness, version, lineage, or audit metadata so operators and clients can distinguish current, pending, and degraded state.

deepDives.title: Sink correctness and replay
points: For the batch and streaming analytics platform, accepted offsets, checkpoint state, and sink writes must advance together.
Keep this concern off unrelated request paths and partition it by the batch and streaming analytics platform access key.
Expose freshness, version, lineage, or audit metadata so operators and clients can distinguish current, pending, and degraded state.

tradeoffs.title: Event-time correctness versus latency
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use watermarks and bounded lateness for correct windows, then expose provisional results while waiting for late events.
tradeoffs.caution: Waiting indefinitely for stragglers makes the dashboard unusable; dropping them silently makes aggregates untrustworthy.

tradeoffs.title: Shared stream engine versus isolated jobs
tradeoffs.recommendation: Share the platform control plane but isolate hot or high-value jobs with independent queues and checkpoints.
tradeoffs.caution: One overloaded topology should not delay unrelated tenants or sinks.

tradeoffs.title: Reprocessing versus deduplicated sinks
tradeoffs.recommendation: Make replay a first-class operation and require sink idempotency keys or transactional commits.
tradeoffs.caution: Replaying compute without sink deduplication creates duplicate actions and aggregates.

commonMistakes: Advancing offsets before durable checkpoint and sink commit.
Treating processing time as event time for out-of-order data.
Allowing one hot partition to starve all jobs.
Hiding incomplete windows and late-event corrections.
Making replay an ad hoc manual database operation.

followUps.question: What happens when a worker fails after processing but before checkpointing?
followUps.answer: The worker resumes from the prior checkpoint and reprocesses the bounded interval; deduplicated sinks make the retry safe.

followUps.question: How do you handle a hot key?
followUps.answer: Detect skew, repartition or salt the key where semantics allow it, isolate the affected job, and expose lag instead of dropping events.

followUps.question: How do you prove output correctness?
followUps.answer: Compare source counts, checkpoint offsets, sink counts, watermarks, and replay results on sampled windows before promoting a result.

rubric.description: The answer defines source contracts, event-time semantics, checkpoints, backpressure, replay, and sink correctness, scale, latency, durability, authorization, and failure behavior.
Entities and keys make the batch and streaming analytics platform state, versions, lifecycle, and derived projections explicit.
Partitioning, queues, backpressure, cache behavior, hot-key handling, and bounded work are explicit.
Idempotency, replay, recovery, degraded behavior, observability, and auditability protect the primary contract.
The candidate can explain the batch and streaming analytics platform consistency boundary, asynchronous work, and operational limits.
